cards.q: Why must .env never be committed?
cards.a: It holds credentials. Git history is permanent, and public repositories are scanned for keys within minutes of a push.

cards.q: What does a virtual environment isolate?
cards.a: Installed packages and the interpreter. Not your data, not the operating system's libraries, and not your git history.

cards.q: Why is the target column blank at the moment you would use the row?
cards.a: Because the target is a fact about t + h, and at t it has not happened yet. Training rows are built from history where t + h is already known; serving rows never have it.
cards.n: Lesson 1, The question: what are we predicting. Check yourself.

cards.q: Why three separate models rather than one model with a 'horizon' column?
cards.a: Simplicity and honest early stopping: each horizon stops training where its own validation score peaks, and the three thresholds are chosen independently. A single model is possible and slightly more coherent across horizons, at the cost of one more feature to get wrong.
cards.n: Lesson 1, The question: what are we predicting. Check yourself.

cards.q: Why not output yes or no?
cards.a: The cost of a false alarm and of a miss are not equal and are not known when the model is trained. A probability defers that decision to a threshold chosen later, and can be evaluated for honesty (calibration).
cards.n: Lesson 1, The question: what are we predicting. Check yourself.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "The model predicts crashes."?
cards.a: It predicts slow episodes; most are propagation of a jam that already exists somewhere downstream, or the daily build-up.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 1, The question: what are we predicting.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "Accuracy is the score."?
cards.a: With 5 % positives, always saying 'not slow' is 95 % accurate. Average precision and recall at a threshold are the scores.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 1, The question: what are we predicting.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "More horizons are free."?
cards.a: Each horizon is a separate, harder problem; skill at 60 minutes is modest and must be shown against persistence.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 1, The question: what are we predicting.

cards.q: Explain the idea of lesson 1: The question: what are we predicting?
cards.a: A prediction problem has four parts. The unit: one station at one 5-minute timestamp. The inputs: everything known at that moment, and nothing after it. The target: a yes-or-no fact about the future, here 'the station is inside a slow episode h minutes later', with h in {15, 30, 60}. The metric: how guesses are scored.
cards.h: → the idea in three or four plain sentences
cards.n: Formally this is supervised binary classification on a panel indexed by (station s, time t). The feature vector x_{s,t} is a function of the information available at t, written F_t;

cards.q: Why does occupancy matter if you already have speed?
cards.a: Speed alone cannot tell a nearly empty road from a dense one moving at the same speed. Occupancy stands in for density, and density is what predicts breakdown.

cards.q: What does % Observed = 20 mean for a row?
cards.a: Only a fifth of the samples in that 5 minutes were real; the rest of the row was filled in by PeMS's imputer. Treat the row as missing for labels and carry the fraction as a feature.

cards.q: Why can the poller miss an incident entirely?
cards.a: It samples the feed every 15 minutes; an event that is created and cleared between two polls never appears. Start times are also only known to within one poll.

cards.q: Why does X @ w compute every row's score?
cards.a: Each row of X dotted with w is one row's weighted sum; the product does all rows in one operation.

cards.q: What does a positive semidefinite Hessian buy you?
cards.a: Convexity. Every local minimum is global, so gradient descent cannot get stuck.
cards.n: Topic: Linear algebra: vectors, dot products, matrices. Check yourself.

cards.q: Why the negative gradient?
cards.a: The gradient points toward increasing loss. Learning wants the opposite direction.
cards.n: Topic: Calculus: derivatives, the chain rule, gradients. Check yourself.

cards.q: What is backpropagation in one sentence?
cards.a: The chain rule applied in reverse order along the computation graph, reusing intermediate results.
cards.n: Topic: Calculus: derivatives, the chain rule, gradients. Check yourself.

cards.q: Why is the profile a median and not a mean?
cards.a: A few outage days with speed 0 or an imputed 70 would drag a mean; the median ignores them.
cards.n: Topic: Probability and statistics: distributions, medians, likelihood. Check yourself.

cards.q: What does the likelihood measure?
cards.a: How probable the observed data are under a candidate model. Maximizing it picks the model that explains the data best.
cards.n: Topic: Probability and statistics: distributions, medians, likelihood. Check yourself.

cards.q: Why cross-entropy and not squared error?
cards.a: Cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of the Bernoulli model and is convex in the weights; squared error on a sigmoid output is not convex and its gradient vanishes when the model is confidently wrong.
cards.n: Lesson 7, Logistic regression from scratch: the math the model runs on. Check yourself.

cards.q: What does the bias do?
cards.a: It sets the probability when all features are zero (after standardization, the average row). Without it the model cannot match the base rate.
cards.n: Lesson 7, Logistic regression from scratch: the math the model runs on. Check yourself.

cards.q: Why does the gradient check matter if the code is short?
cards.a: A sign error or a missing division by n produces a loop that still decreases the loss slowly, and you would never know. Finite differences catch it in one line.
cards.n: Lesson 7, Logistic regression from scratch: the math the model runs on. Check yourself.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "A bigger learning rate learns faster."?
cards.a: Past a limit set by the curvature it diverges; the loss goes up, not down.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 7, Logistic regression from scratch: the math the model runs on.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "The weights say which feature matters most."?
cards.a: Only after standardization, and only for the linear part; correlated features share weight arbitrarily.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 7, Logistic regression from scratch: the math the model runs on.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "Logistic regression is obsolete."?
cards.a: It is the calibration-friendly baseline every other model must beat, and it is inside every neural network's output layer.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 7, Logistic regression from scratch: the math the model runs on.

cards.q: Explain the idea of lesson 7: Logistic regression from scratch: the math the model runs on
cards.a: Score z = w·x + b. Probability p = σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)). Loss for one row, the cross-entropy: −[y ln p + (1 − y) ln(1 − p)], which is small when confident and right and huge when confident and wrong.
cards.h: → the idea in three or four plain sentences
cards.n: Logistic regression is maximum likelihood for a Bernoulli outcome with a logit-linear mean.

cards.q: Why filter inside each chunk rather than after concatenating?
cards.a: Concatenating first means holding the whole district-day in memory, about 1.3 million rows and every column. Filtering per chunk keeps the peak under a few hundred megabytes.

cards.q: Why drop the ambiguous November hour instead of resolving it?

cards.q: Why does the relative label ignore the rush hour?
cards.a: Because the profile is the typical speed at that slot, and at 5 pm the typical speed is already slow. A ratio near 1 is 'normal for now', whatever the absolute speed.
cards.n: Lesson 4, Labels: what does 'slow' mean. Check yourself.

cards.q: What happens to the label if the profile is computed on all data?
cards.a: Test-period speeds shape the profile that defines training labels, a leak. The evaluation then overstates skill in a way that is very hard to see.
cards.n: Lesson 4, Labels: what does 'slow' mean. Check yourself.

cards.q: Why three consecutive steps?
cards.a: To reject single noisy readings. It also shifts the label window: the label at t + h depends on speeds at t + h − 2 through t + h, which must not overlap the features at t.
cards.n: Lesson 4, Labels: what does 'slow' mean. Check yourself.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "The median profile is the free-flow speed."?
cards.a: It is the typical speed, which at rush hour is far below free flow. Free flow is the 85th percentile.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 4, Labels: what does 'slow' mean.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "Threshold 0.6 is a fact."?
cards.a: It is a choice that sets prevalence and difficulty; version it.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 4, Labels: what does 'slow' mean.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "A label is ground truth."?
cards.a: It is a derived quantity with its own estimation error, concentrated at the boundary.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 4, Labels: what does 'slow' mean.

cards.q: Explain the idea of lesson 4: Labels: what does 'slow' mean?
cards.a: Three formulas. profile(s, slot, daytype) = median of speed over training days. ratio = speed / profile. is_slow = ratio < 0.6, and label = 1 when is_slow holds for three consecutive steps, the window ending at the row's own time.
cards.h: → the idea in three or four plain sentences
cards.n: The label is a deterministic function of the series and an estimated profile, so the profile is part of the model.

cards.q: Why sin and cos of the minute rather than the minute itself?
cards.a: The minute jumps from 1439 to 0 at midnight; a model would see a cliff. The pair (sin, cos) is continuous around the circle and two columns are needed because sin alone maps two different times to the same value.
cards.n: Lesson 5, Features: turning the past into columns. Check yourself.

cards.q: Why does the target use a negative shift?
cards.a: shift(−6) pulls the value six rows later into the current row: the label thirty minutes ahead, aligned with the features at t.
cards.n: Lesson 5, Features: turning the past into columns. Check yourself.

cards.q: Why keep NaN for LightGBM but impute for the network?
cards.a: Trees route missing values down a learned branch; a network multiplies NaN into every weight. Impute, and add an indicator so the network can still know the value was missing.
cards.n: Lesson 5, Features: turning the past into columns. Check yourself.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "More features always help."?
cards.a: Correlated features hurt linear models and slow trees; every feature is another thing to monitor for drift.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 5, Features: turning the past into columns.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "Realized weather is a fine training feature."?
cards.a: At serving time only the forecast exists. Train on what you will have.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 5, Features: turning the past into columns.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "Rolling windows are safe."?
cards.a: Only trailing windows are; centered windows look ahead.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 5, Features: turning the past into columns.

cards.q: Explain the idea of lesson 5: Features: turning the past into columns
cards.a: Lags come from a shift within each station on the full grid: df.groupby('station_id')['speed'].shift(k). Rolling statistics from .rolling(6).mean() where 6 steps is 30 minutes. The slope is speed_lag_0 − speed_lag_3.
cards.h: → the idea in three or four plain sentences
cards.n: Every feature must be F_t-measurable, a function of information available at t.

cards.q: Why is persistence such a strong baseline at 15 minutes?
cards.a: Speed five minutes ago is highly autocorrelated with speed in fifteen; jams rarely appear from nothing inside one step. Skill over persistence grows with horizon.
cards.n: Lesson 6, Baselines and honest evaluation. Check yourself.

cards.q: Why bootstrap over days rather than rows?
cards.a: Rows within a day are dependent; resampling rows pretends they are independent and gives intervals that are far too narrow.
cards.n: Lesson 6, Baselines and honest evaluation. Check yourself.

cards.q: What does a high ROC-AUC with a low AP tell you?
cards.a: The model ranks negatives well below positives on average, but the top of the ranking, which is what alerts use, is still polluted with false positives. Under imbalance ROC-AUC is the flattering one.
cards.n: Lesson 6, Baselines and honest evaluation. Check yourself.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "Cross-validation is always better than a single split."?
cards.a: Shuffled CV on a time series leaks and reports fantasy scores; only forward splits are valid here.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 6, Baselines and honest evaluation.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "Beating the baseline once is enough."?
cards.a: Report it per horizon and per fold; a model can beat persistence at 60 minutes and lose at 15.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 6, Baselines and honest evaluation.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "Calibration is a detail."?
cards.a: It is the difference between a probability and a score, and the threshold rule assumes a probability.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 6, Baselines and honest evaluation.

cards.q: Explain the idea of lesson 6: Baselines and honest evaluation
cards.a: The confusion matrix gives true and false positives and negatives. Precision = TP / (TP + FP); recall = TP / (TP + FN); F1 is their harmonic mean. Sliding the threshold traces the precision-recall curve; its area is average precision (AP), the headline metric here. ROC-AUC exists too but looks flattering under imbalance because true negatives are cheap.
cards.h: → the idea in three or four plain sentences
cards.n: Shuffled K-fold is wrong for a time series because autocorrelation places near-copies of every test row in the training fold, and because the estimand is future performance, which only forward valida…

cards.q: What does min_data_in_leaf = 200 protect against?
cards.a: A leaf that isolates a handful of rows fits their noise; 200 forces every leaf to summarize a real population, which is regularization by construction.
cards.n: Lesson 8, Gradient boosted trees. Check yourself.

cards.q: Why pass station_id as a categorical rather than as an integer?
cards.a: As an integer the tree would split on 'id < 4123', which is meaningless. As a categorical it can group stations by behavior.
cards.n: Lesson 8, Gradient boosted trees. Check yourself.

cards.q: Why is early stopping done on the validation split and not on training loss?
cards.a: Training loss keeps falling as trees are added; validation AP peaks and then declines as the ensemble fits noise. The peak is the model you want.
cards.n: Lesson 8, Gradient boosted trees. Check yourself.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "More trees always help."?
cards.a: Past the validation peak they hurt, which is what early stopping finds.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 8, Gradient boosted trees.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "Feature importance shows causation."?
cards.a: It shows what the trees used; a proxy for the cause ranks as high as the cause.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 8, Gradient boosted trees.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "Tree scores are probabilities."?
cards.a: They are ranked well and calibrated badly; isotonic regression fixes that in lesson 11.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 8, Gradient boosted trees.

cards.q: Explain the idea of lesson 8: Gradient boosted trees
cards.a: A tree chooses the split that most reduces the mix of classes in its leaves (the gain). Depth and the number of leaves control how detailed it can be. Boosting: start with a constant F₀, then repeatedly fit a small tree h_m to the residuals (for logistic loss, y − p) and set F_m = F_{m−1} + η h_m.
cards.h: → the idea in three or four plain sentences
cards.n: Gradient boosting is gradient descent in function space (Friedman, 2001).

cards.q: Why does random search often beat grid search?

cards.q: Why must the test split stay untouched during tuning?

cards.q: Why is cross-entropy the loss for classification?

cards.q: What does mutual information capture that correlation misses?

cards.q: Why is the downstream neighbor more informative than the upstream one for the next 30 minutes?
cards.a: Queues grow backwards. A slow downstream station means the wave is heading toward you; a slow upstream station means it has already passed.
cards.n: Lesson 10, Jams move: sequences, neighbors and the road graph. Check yourself.

cards.q: What limits how far ahead neighbors can help?
cards.a: Distance to the disturbance divided by the wave speed. Beyond that horizon nothing on the road yet carries the information.
cards.n: Lesson 10, Jams move: sequences, neighbors and the road graph. Check yourself.

cards.q: Why share the GRU across stations?
cards.a: One set of weights sees a hundred times more data, and the dynamics of a queue are the same physics everywhere; station identity can be added as an embedding if needed.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "Traffic is random."?
cards.a: Propagation is mechanical and fast to learn; what is hard is the onset of the first disturbance.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 10, Jams move: sequences, neighbors and the road graph.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "The graph model replaces the physics."?
cards.a: It learns the physics from data; encoding wave direction helps it learn faster.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 10, Jams move: sequences, neighbors and the road graph.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "Longer windows are better."?
cards.a: Beyond an hour the extra history mostly adds noise; the calendar carries the slow signal.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 10, Jams move: sequences, neighbors and the road graph.

cards.q: Explain the idea of lesson 10: Jams move: sequences, neighbors and the road graph
cards.a: Time series vocabulary: autocorrelation (speed now versus five minutes ago correlates at about 0.9), seasonality (daily and weekly), lags as features; persistence is strong precisely because autocorrelation is strong.
cards.h: → the idea in three or four plain sentences
cards.n: Kinematic wave theory (Lighthill-Whitham-Richards): conservation ∂k/∂t + ∂q/∂x = 0 with a fundamental diagram q = Q(k). A discontinuity between states 1 and 2 moves at w = (q₂ − q₁)/(k₂ − k₁);

cards.q: Why calibrate on the validation split and not on training?
cards.a: The model has fit the training rows; its confidence there is meaningless. Calibration needs rows the model has not seen, and the test split must stay untouched for the final report.
cards.n: Lesson 11, From scores to alerts: calibration, thresholds, lead time. Check yourself.

cards.q: What does a lead time of zero or negative mean?
cards.a: The first alert came at or after the episode began: the model saw the jam, it did not foresee it. Expect that for crash-initiated episodes.
cards.n: Lesson 11, From scores to alerts: calibration, thresholds, lead time. Check yourself.

cards.q: Why count false alarms per station-day and not per row?
cards.a: A driver experiences alerts per trip, not per 5-minute row; a station firing twenty times in one hour is one bad hour, not twenty errors.
cards.n: Lesson 11, From scores to alerts: calibration, thresholds, lead time. Check yourself.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "0.5 is the natural threshold."?
cards.a: It is only right when a false alarm and a miss cost the same, which they never do.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 11, From scores to alerts: calibration, thresholds, lead time.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "Calibration fixes ranking."?
cards.a: It is monotone; it changes the numbers, not the order.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 11, From scores to alerts: calibration, thresholds, lead time.

cards.q: What is wrong with: "A high AP means useful alerts."?
cards.a: Only the episode metrics, lead time and false alarms, say that.
cards.n: A common misconception from lesson 11, From scores to alerts: calibration, thresholds, lead time.

cards.q: Explain the idea of lesson 11: From scores to alerts: calibration, thresholds, lead time
cards.a: Reliability diagram: bin rows by predicted probability, plot the observed share of positives per bin; the gap is calibration error. Two fixes fit on the validation split: Platt scaling (a sigmoid on the score) and isotonic regression (a monotone step function). Isotonic is more flexible and needs more data.
cards.h: → the idea in three or four plain sentences
cards.n: Proper scoring rules decompose into calibration and refinement; a model can rank perfectly and be badly calibrated, which is the tree-ensemble case.

cards.q: Explain the idea of lesson 9: Neural networks and backpropagation, on the M1
cards.a: Forward pass: h = ReLU(W₁x + b₁), p = σ(w₂·h + b₂). Loss: cross-entropy. Backward pass: ∂L/∂w₂ = (p − y) h; ∂L/∂h = (p − y) w₂; through ReLU multiply by 1 where the pre-activation was positive and 0 elsewhere; ∂L/∂W₁ = δ₁ xᵀ.
cards.h: → the idea in three or four plain sentences
cards.n: Backpropagation is reverse-mode automatic differentiation on a computational graph: one forward and one backward pass give every parameter's gradient at a cost independent of parameter count.

cards.q: What does the KL term in a VAE do?

cards.q: What distinguishes RL from supervised learning?
cards.a: There are no correct labels, only rewards, and the agent's actions change the data it sees.

cards.a: Immediate feedback and no state transitions make evaluation and safety tractable; most product decisions look like that.

cards.q: Why does adjusting for a collider cause bias?
cards.a: Conditioning on a common effect of two variables induces an association between them that does not exist causally.

cards.q: What does randomization buy?
cards.a: Treated and untreated groups are comparable on everything, measured or not, so the difference in outcomes is the causal effect on average.
cards.n: Topic: Causal inference: from correlation to intervention. Check yourself.

cards.q: Why can a model be calibrated for every group and still have unequal error rates?

cards.q: What does differential privacy guarantee?
cards.a: That any single person's data changes the released output's distribution by at most a bounded factor, whatever else an attacker knows.
cards.n: Topic: Fairness, privacy and ethics: what a model owes people. Check yourself.

cards.q: Why is offline evaluation of a recommender biased?
cards.a: Logged feedback exists only for items that were shown; items never shown have no data, and the log reflects the old policy's choices.

cards.q: What does NDCG reward?

cards.q: A key takeaway from Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction (Murphy)?
cards.a: One vocabulary (likelihood, prior, posterior, predictive, decision) covers every model in the book, which is why the book is worth reading front to back.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Part I foundations: introduction; probability (univariate and multivariate models, Bayes' rule, exponential families, transformations, Monte Carlo);

cards.q: A key takeaway from The Elements of Statistical Learning (Hastie, Tibshirani, Friedman)?
cards.a: Chapter 7 (assessment) and chapter 10 (boosting) explain why LightGBM works and how to tune it; read those first.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Chapters: introduction; overview of supervised learning (least squares and nearest neighbours, statistical decision theory, the curse of dimensionality, bias-variance);

cards.q: A key takeaway from Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms (Shalev-Shwartz, Ben-David)?
cards.a: Learnability requires a restricted class; generalisation bounds trade class richness (VC, Rademacher) against sample size.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Part I foundations: a gentle start (ERM, overfitting, finite hypothesis classes); a formal learning model (PAC, agnostic PAC, the realisability assumption);

cards.q: A key takeaway from Convex Optimization (Boyd, Vandenberghe)?
cards.a: Convexity is the property that makes a problem solvable exactly; learn to recognise and preserve it.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Part I theory: convex sets (affine and convex sets, operations that preserve convexity, generalised inequalities, separating and supporting hyperplanes, dual cones);

cards.q: A key takeaway from CS229 lecture notes (Stanford)?
cards.a: The GLM construction is the single most reusable derivation: it generates linear, logistic, Poisson and softmax regression from one recipe.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Main notes: supervised learning (linear regression, LMS, normal equations, probabilistic interpretation, locally weighted regression, logistic regression, Newton's method, GLMs and expon…

cards.q: A key takeaway from CS224W: Machine Learning with Graphs (Stanford)?
cards.a: A GNN layer is message, aggregate, update; every architecture is a choice of those three.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Lectures and slides: introduction (why graphs, applications, representations);

cards.q: A key takeaway from A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction (Angelopoulos, Bates)?
cards.a: Any model plus a calibration set gives valid prediction sets in three lines; the guarantee needs exchangeability, not correctness of the model.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Sections: conformal prediction (the recipe with a heuristic notion of uncertainty, a score function, a calibration set, the quantile, and prediction sets that contain the truth with the…

cards.q: A key takeaway from Adaptive Conformal Inference Under Distribution Shift (Gibbs, Candès, 2021)?
cards.a: Coverage under shift comes from feedback control, not from the model.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: The paper: setting (online prediction with a model that may be arbitrarily wrong and data whose distribution shifts over time);

cards.q: A key takeaway from Statistical Rethinking lectures and course materials (McElreath)?
cards.a: Draw the DAG first; the elemental confounds tell you what to adjust for and what to leave alone.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Lecture series and course materials: science before statistics (models as golems, causal thinking, DAGs);

cards.q: A key takeaway from Probabilistic Programming and Bayesian Methods for Hackers (Davidson-Pilon)?
cards.a: Write the generative story, then let the sampler invert it; that is the whole workflow.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Chapters (as notebooks): introduction (the Bayesian state of mind, Bayes' theorem, probability distributions, a text-message change-point example in PyMC);

cards.q: A key takeaway from A Visual Exploration of Gaussian Processes (Distill, 2019)?
cards.a: A kernel is a statement about function shape; choose it by what you know about the function.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: An interactive article: multivariate Gaussians (marginalisation and conditioning); Gaussian processes as distributions over functions defined by a mean and a kernel;

cards.q: A key takeaway from Foundations of Machine Learning (Mohri, Rostamizadeh, Talwalkar), 2nd edition?
cards.a: Rademacher complexity is the one tool that yields most bounds in the book, so learn its symmetrisation proof.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Chapters: introduction; the PAC learning framework (guarantees for finite consistent and inconsistent hypothesis sets, generalities such as deterministic versus stochastic scenarios and…

cards.q: A key takeaway from PyTorch Geometric documentation?
cards.a: edge_index in COO plus a features matrix is the whole representation; get comfortable building it from a station adjacency table.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Get started (installation, introduction by example: data handling of graphs, common benchmark datasets, mini-batches, data transforms, learning methods on graphs);

cards.q: A key takeaway from Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd edition (Gelman, Carlin, Stern, Dunson, Vehtari, Rubin)?
cards.a: Model, condition, check, expand: the workflow matters more than any single model.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Part I fundamentals: probability and inference; single-parameter models (binomial, normal, Poisson, exponential, prior distributions, noninformative and weakly informative priors);

cards.q: A key takeaway from Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning (Rasmussen, Williams)?
cards.a: The marginal likelihood is the principled way to set kernel hyperparameters and it penalises complexity on its own.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Chapters: introduction; regression (weight-space view with Bayesian linear regression and feature projections, function-space view, varying the hyperparameters, decision theory for regre…

cards.q: A key takeaway from Deep Learning (Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville)?
cards.a: Chapters 6 to 8 (feedforward, regularisation, optimisation) are the durable core; read them fully.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Part I applied math and ML basics: linear algebra; probability and information theory;

cards.q: A key takeaway from Graph WaveNet (Wu et al., IJCAI 2019)?
cards.a: Learning the graph (adaptive adjacency) beats trusting the road graph; the two together are best.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: The paper: motivation (spatial dependencies in traffic are not fully captured by the road-distance graph, and RNN-based temporal models are slow);

cards.q: A key takeaway from METR-LA and PEMS-BAY datasets (DCRNN repository)?
cards.a: The METR-LA and PEMS-BAY format, split and masked metrics are the shared language of traffic forecasting; use the same format for Fremont so results are comparable.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: The repository for Diffusion Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network: the two datasets (METR-LA, 207 loop detectors in Los Angeles County, four months of five-minute speeds in 2012;

cards.q: A key takeaway from ETA Prediction with Graph Neural Networks in Google Maps (Derrow-Pinion et al., 2021)?
cards.a: Multi-level supervision (segment, supersegment, route) makes the parts consistent with the whole.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: The paper: the problem (estimated time of arrival for a route as a sum over road segments, with a supersegment graph that groups segments);

cards.q: State the formula for loss (from The repo's own 00_CONCEPTS.md and…).
cards.a: loss = -mean(y*log(p) + (1-y)*log(1-p))
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for The repo's own 00_CONCEPTS.md and 05_PLAN_COMBINED_DATASETS.md.

cards.q: State the formula for a·b (from Khan Academy: Linear algebra…).
cards.a: a·b = Σ aᵢbᵢ = |a||b| cos θ
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Khan Academy: Linear algebra, Differential calculus, Statistics and probability.

cards.q: State the formula for x_{t+1} (from Mathematics for Machine Learning…).
cards.a: x_{t+1} = x_t − γ ∇f(x_t)ᵀ
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Mathematics for Machine Learning (Deisenroth, Faisal, Ong), chapters 2–7.

cards.q: State the formula for p-value (from OpenIntro Statistics).
cards.a: p-value = P(statistic at least as extreme | H₀)
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for OpenIntro Statistics.

cards.q: State the formula for L (from Machine Learning Specialization…).
cards.a: L = −y log f(x) − (1 − y) log(1 − f(x))
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Machine Learning Specialization (Andrew Ng), courses 1 and 2.

cards.q: State the formula for F1 (from Machine Learning Specialization…).
cards.a: F1 = 2PR/(P + R)
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Machine Learning Specialization (Andrew Ng), courses 1 and 2.

cards.q: State the formula for prediction bias (from Google's Machine Learning Crash Course).
cards.a: prediction bias = mean(predictions) − mean(labels)
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Google's Machine Learning Crash Course.

cards.q: State the formula for w*_leaf (from The boosting papers: Friedman (2001)…).
cards.a: w*_leaf = −Σ_{i∈leaf} g_i / (Σ_{i∈leaf} h_i + λ)
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for The boosting papers: Friedman (2001), XGBoost (2016), LightGBM (2017).

cards.q: State the formula for MASE (from Forecasting: Principles and Practice…).
cards.a: MASE = MAE / MAE_naive_in-sample
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Forecasting: Principles and Practice, the Python edition (Hyndman, Athanasopoulos), chapters 1–5, 7, 9.

cards.q: State the formula for y_{t+h} (from Kaggle Learn: Time Series).
cards.a: y_{t+h} = f_h(y_t, y_{t−1}, …, x_t) (direct strategy, one model per h)
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Kaggle Learn: Time Series.

cards.q: State the formula for wave speed w (from traffic-simulation.de and its model…).
cards.a: wave speed w = Δq/Δk between two traffic states
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for traffic-simulation.de and its model documentation (Treiber, Kesting).

cards.q: State the formula for RMSLE (from Kaggle: Store Sales, Time Series…).
cards.a: RMSLE = √( mean (log(1 + ŷ) − log(1 + y))² )
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Kaggle: Store Sales, Time Series Forecasting competition.

cards.q: State the formula for RMSSE (from The M5 forecasting competition and its…).
cards.a: RMSSE = √( mean_h (y_{t+h} − ŷ_{t+h})² / mean_t (y_t − y_{t−1})² )
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for The M5 forecasting competition and its findings (Makridakis, Spiliotis, Assimakopoulos).

cards.q: State the formula for conv output size (from CS231n: Convolutional Neural Networks…).
cards.a: conv output size = (W − F + 2P)/S + 1
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for CS231n: Convolutional Neural Networks for Visual Recognition, course notes.

cards.q: State the formula for softmax loss L_i (from CS231n: Convolutional Neural Networks…).
cards.a: softmax loss L_i = −log( e^{f_{y_i}} / Σ_j e^{f_j} )
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for CS231n: Convolutional Neural Networks for Visual Recognition, course notes.

cards.q: State the formula for lr (from Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et…).
cards.a: lr = d_model^{−0.5} · min(step^{−0.5}, step · warmup^{−1.5})
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017).

cards.q: State the formula for perplexity (from Speech and Language Processing, 3rd…).
cards.a: perplexity = P(w₁…w_N)^{−1/N}
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Speech and Language Processing, 3rd edition draft (Jurafsky, Martin).

cards.q: State the formula for L_DDPM (from The generative-model papers: VAE…).
cards.a: L_DDPM = E ‖ε − ε_θ(√ᾱ_t x_0 + √(1 − ᾱ_t) ε, t)‖²
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for The generative-model papers: VAE (Kingma, Welling, 2013), GAN (Goodfellow et al., 2014), DDPM (Ho, Jain, Abbeel, 2020).

cards.q: State the formula for L_simple (from What are Diffusion Models? (Weng…).
cards.a: L_simple = E_{t, x_0, ε} ‖ ε − ε_θ(√ᾱ_t x_0 + √(1 − ᾱ_t) ε, t) ‖²
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for What are Diffusion Models? (Weng, Lil'Log).

cards.q: State the formula for score (from The ML Test Score (Breck, Cai…).
cards.a: score = min over categories of Σ_tests {0, 0.5 manual, 1 automated}
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for The ML Test Score (Breck, Cai, Nielsen, Salib, Sculley, 2017).

cards.q: State the formula for cross-entropy (from Probabilistic Machine Learning: An…).
cards.a: cross-entropy = H(p) + KL(p || q)
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction (Murphy).

cards.q: State the formula for alpha_{t+1} (from Adaptive Conformal Inference Under…).
cards.a: alpha_{t+1} = alpha_t + gamma (alpha - err_t), err_t = 1{ Y_t not in C_t }
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Adaptive Conformal Inference Under Distribution Shift (Gibbs, Candès, 2021).

cards.q: State the formula for WAIC (from Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd edition…).
cards.a: WAIC = -2 ( lppd - p_WAIC )
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd edition (Gelman, Carlin, Stern, Dunson, Vehtari, Rubin).

cards.q: State the formula for Matérn nu (from Gaussian Processes for Machine…).
cards.a: Matérn nu = 3/2: k(r) = sigma^2 (1 + sqrt(3) r / l) exp( -sqrt(3) r / l )
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning (Rasmussen, Williams).

cards.q: State the formula for masked MAE (from METR-LA and PEMS-BAY datasets (DCRNN…).
cards.a: masked MAE = sum_{i: y_i != 0} |y_i - y_hat_i| / count(y_i != 0)
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for METR-LA and PEMS-BAY datasets (DCRNN repository).

cards.q: State the formula for route ETA (from ETA Prediction with Graph Neural…).
cards.a: route ETA = sum over supersegments of predicted traversal time
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for ETA Prediction with Graph Neural Networks in Google Maps (Derrow-Pinion et al., 2021).

cards.q: Define: Terminal
cards.a: The text window (the Terminal app on a Mac) where you type commands and press return instead of clicking. Every script in the course is started from it.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Shell
cards.a: The program inside the terminal that reads your commands; on a modern Mac it is zsh. Paths, pipes and environment variables are shell ideas.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Command
cards.a: One line typed into the shell: a program name followed by its arguments, such as python 02_collect_events.py.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Path
cards.a: The address of a file or folder. Absolute paths start at the root (/Users/you/Traffic1/data); relative paths start from the folder you are in (data/pems_raw). cd changes the current folder; ls lists it.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Pipe |
cards.a: Sends the output of one command into the next, so zcat file.gz | head -3 shows three lines of a compressed file without unpacking it.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Environment variable
cards.a: A named value the shell keeps and passes to programs, such as a password or an API key set with export PEMS_USERNAME=.... A .env file lists them so scripts can load them.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Python
cards.a: The programming language the course uses. It reads a text file of instructions and runs them one line at a time.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Script
cards.a: A file of Python code ending in .py, run with python name.py. The numbered files in Traffic1 (10_clean_pems.py and so on) are the pipeline's scripts.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Library (package)
cards.a: A bundle of ready-made code you load with import. pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, LightGBM and PyTorch are libraries.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: pip
cards.a: The tool that installs Python libraries: pip install pandas. requirements.txt lists everything the project needs so pip install -r requirements.txt installs it all.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Virtual environment (venv)
cards.a: A private copy of Python and its libraries for one project, so projects do not fight over versions. Create it once, activate it, install into it, and point VS Code and launchd at its Python.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: arm64 / Apple silicon
cards.a: The M-series chips in modern Macs. Python and its libraries must be the arm64 builds to use the chip well; platform.machine() must print arm64.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Jupyter notebook
cards.a: An app that runs Python one cell at a time and shows results, tables and plots under each cell. Good for looking at data; scripts are better for the pipeline.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: VS Code
cards.a: A free code editor. Point it at the venv's Python so it runs and checks code with the right libraries.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Git
cards.a: The version-control tool. It records snapshots (commits) of your files so you can see history, undo, and branch. GitHub hosts repositories online.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Repository (repo)
cards.a: A folder whose history git tracks. Traffic1 is one. .gitignore lists what git must never record, such as data/ and .env.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Commit, branch, push
cards.a: A commit is one saved snapshot with a message; a branch is a named line of commits; push copies your commits to GitHub.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: CSV
cards.a: Comma-separated values: a text table, one row per line, commas between fields. Easy to read, slow and large.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Parquet
cards.a: A compressed, column-by-column file format for tables. Small on disk, fast to load, keeps data types. The course stores every cleaned table this way.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: gzip (.gz)
cards.a: A compression format. PeMS files arrive gzipped; zcat prints them decompressed and pandas can read them directly.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: JSON
cards.a: A text format for lists and dictionaries ({"h": 30, "p": 0.42}) that every language can read. Used for thresholds, feature lists and the live predictions file.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: YAML / plist / XML
cards.a: Other text formats for settings. A launchd plist is XML: keys and values inside angle-bracket tags.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: launchd
cards.a: macOS's built-in scheduler. A plist in ~/Library/LaunchAgents tells it to run a program every N seconds or at boot, with logs to named files.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Log
cards.a: A text file a program appends lines to as it runs, so you can see what happened after the fact. Every stage in the course writes one line with its name, time and memory.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: API key / token
cards.a: A secret string that identifies you to a web service such as 511. Kept in .env, never in code or git.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Polling
cards.a: Asking a server for its current data on a schedule, as the 511 collector does every few minutes.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: PeMS
cards.a: Caltrans' Performance Measurement System: the archive of freeway detector readings for California, published as daily text files per district.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: 511
cards.a: The Bay Area traveller-information service; its API lists current incidents (crashes, stalls, closures) with times and locations.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Station (detector)
cards.a: One sensor site on the freeway, identified by a number. It reports flow, occupancy and speed every five minutes.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Mainline (ML)
cards.a: A detector on the through lanes, as opposed to an on-ramp, off-ramp or HOV lane. The course uses mainline stations only.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Postmile
cards.a: A station's distance along its freeway, used to put stations in driving order and find neighbors.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Upstream / downstream
cards.a: Upstream is where traffic comes from; downstream is where it is going. A jam downstream reaches you soon.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Registry
cards.a: The course's small curated table of the Fremont stations with their neighbors, built once from the PeMS meta file.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Flow
cards.a: Vehicles counted passing the detector in the interval.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Occupancy
cards.a: The fraction of the interval the sensor was covered by a vehicle; a stand-in for how densely packed the road is.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Speed
cards.a: Average speed in miles per hour over the interval.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: pct_obs
cards.a: The percentage of a five-minute row that came from real observations rather than PeMS's fill-in estimates. Below 50 the row is mostly guesswork.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Five-minute row / slot
cards.a: One reading per station per five minutes: 288 per day. The slot is the position in the day, 0 to 287.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Grid
cards.a: Every station × every slot, with no gaps. Missing readings are kept as NaN rows, never skipped, so shifts and windows stay aligned.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Timestamp
cards.a: A moment in time as a datetime value. Stored in UTC in the course; converted to Pacific time only to compute the hour of day.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Timezone, UTC, DST
cards.a: A timezone maps clock readings to moments. UTC is the single world clock. Daylight saving time makes one local hour vanish in spring and repeat in autumn, which the parsing code must handle.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: NaN / NaT
cards.a: Not a number / not a time: the markers for a missing value. Most pandas functions skip them; fillna replaces them.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Imputation
cards.a: Filling a missing value with an estimate. PeMS imputes; the course blanks heavily imputed rows and forward-fills short gaps.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Forward fill
cards.a: Copying the last known value into the following empty slots, up to a limit.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Incident
cards.a: A 511 event: crash, stall, closure, with created, updated and pulled-at times. Its reporting delay limits how much it can help.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Schema
cards.a: The list of a table's columns and their types. Checked before every write.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: pandas
cards.a: The Python library for tables. pd.read_csv, read_parquet, groupby, merge, shift, rolling are its verbs.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: DataFrame / Series
cards.a: A DataFrame is a table with named columns; a Series is one column. Selecting a column gives a Series.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: numpy
cards.a: The library for fast arithmetic on arrays. np.sin, np.mean, X @ w work on whole arrays at once.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: Array / matrix / tensor
cards.a: A grid of numbers: one-dimensional (vector), two-dimensional (matrix), or more. PyTorch calls its arrays tensors.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: Shape
cards.a: The size of each dimension of an array, such as (rows, columns) or (batch, time, channel, station). Most deep-learning bugs are shape bugs.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: Index
cards.a: The row labels of a DataFrame. A MultiIndex has more than one level, such as (station, timestamp). reset_index turns levels back into columns.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: Boolean mask
cards.a: A column of true/false, one per row, used to select rows: df[df.speed < 35].
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: .loc / .iloc
cards.a: Select by label (.loc[row, column]) or by position (.iloc[0]). Assigning to .loc[mask, col] changes only the masked rows.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: groupby
cards.a: Split a table into groups by a key, compute something per group, and combine. groupby("station_id").size() counts rows per station.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: transform
cards.a: A groupby method that returns a result the same length as the input, so it can be stored as a new column.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: merge (join)
cards.a: Line two tables up on shared key columns and combine their other columns. how="left" keeps every row of the left table.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: shift(k)
cards.a: Move a column down by k rows (a lag). A negative k moves it up, which looks into the future: allowed only for targets.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: rolling(n)
cards.a: A window of the last n rows; .mean(), .std(), .sum(), .max() summarize it. Rows must be in time order first.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: pivot
cards.a: Turn a long table (one row per station and time) into a wide one (one row per time, one column per station).
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: Chunking / streaming
cards.a: Reading a file in pieces (chunksize) and keeping only what is needed from each, so memory stays small.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: float32 / int8
cards.a: Number types that use 4 bytes and 1 byte instead of 8. Halving or quartering memory with no real loss for speeds and flags.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: f-string
cards.a: Text with values filled in: f"speed_lag_{k}".
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: List comprehension
cards.a: A one-line loop that builds a list: [c for c in cols if c != "y"].
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: Lambda
cards.a: A small unnamed function written inline: lambda s: s.rolling(3).sum().
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: assert
cards.a: A check that must be true or the program stops with an error. The cheapest safety net; put one before every write.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: Seed (random_state, default_rng(0))
cards.a: A fixed starting point for random numbers, so a run can be repeated exactly.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: matplotlib
cards.a: Python's plotting library. plt.plot, plt.scatter, plt.show.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: Unit
cards.a: The thing a row describes: one station at one timestamp.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Inputs (features)
cards.a: The columns a model reads. Every one must be known at the row's moment.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Target (label)
cards.a: The column the model tries to predict. Here 1 if the station is inside a slow episode h minutes later, else 0.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Horizon
cards.a: How far ahead the prediction looks: 15, 30 or 60 minutes, one model each.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Slow episode
cards.a: Three consecutive five-minute rows with speed below 60 percent of the station's typical speed for that slot and day type.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Profile
cards.a: The typical speed per station, day type and slot, computed as the median over training rows only.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Prevalence
cards.a: The share of rows that are positive. Small here, which is why accuracy is useless and average precision is used.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Leakage
cards.a: Any information from after a row's moment getting into its inputs, or test data influencing training choices. The mistake that makes models look great and then fail.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Feature engineering
cards.a: Deciding and computing the input columns: lags, rolling statistics, time-of-day circle, holidays, neighbor readings.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Lag
cards.a: A value from k steps earlier in the same station's series.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Cyclic encoding
cards.a: Placing a time on a circle with sine and cosine so 23:55 and 00:05 are close.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Split (train / validation / test)
cards.a: Dividing the data by date. The model learns from training, choices are made on validation, and test is scored once at the end.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Baseline
cards.a: The simplest forecast without a model: persistence (the future equals now) and the profile rate (the historical average). Every model must beat them.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Metric
cards.a: How guesses are scored. Average precision, precision, recall, Brier score, lead time and false-alarm rate are the course's metrics.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Precision / recall
cards.a: Precision is the share of alarms that were right; recall is the share of real jams that were alarmed. Raising one usually lowers the other.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Average precision (AP)
cards.a: The area under the precision-recall curve: the prevalence for random guessing, 1.0 for perfect. Not fooled by rare positives.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Threshold (τ)
cards.a: The score above which an alert fires. Chosen on validation to meet a required precision.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Calibration
cards.a: Whether a score of 0.3 really means a 30 percent chance. Checked with a reliability diagram; fixed with isotonic regression.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Brier score
cards.a: Mean squared difference between predicted probability and outcome; lower is better.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Bootstrap
cards.a: Estimating uncertainty by resampling the data many times and recomputing the score. Resample whole days for time series.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Onset, lead time, false alarm
cards.a: An onset is the first row of an episode; lead time is minutes from the first alert to the onset; a false alarm is an alert with no episode in the next hour.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Drift
cards.a: The data slowly changing after training. Measured with the population stability index; confirmed by delayed scoring.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Population stability index (PSI)
cards.a: One number comparing a feature's distribution now with training. Below 0.1 stable, above 0.25 moved.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Model
cards.a: A function from inputs to a score, with parameters set by training.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Parameters (weights) / hyperparameters
cards.a: Parameters are learned from data; hyperparameters (learning rate, number of leaves) are chosen before training.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Logistic regression
cards.a: Weighted sum of features plus bias, squashed by the sigmoid into a probability. The simplest model that outputs a probability.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Sigmoid
cards.a: 1 / (1 + e^(−z)): turns any number into a value between 0 and 1.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Logit
cards.a: The number before the sigmoid. PyTorch's loss takes logits directly for numerical safety.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Loss
cards.a: A number measuring how wrong the model is. Cross-entropy (log loss) for probabilities; training makes it smaller.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Cross-entropy
cards.a: −log p for a true positive, −log(1 − p) for a true negative, averaged. Punishes confident wrong answers heavily.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Gradient
cards.a: The direction in which the loss rises fastest, one number per parameter. Training steps against it.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Gradient descent / mini-batch / epoch / learning rate
cards.a: Repeatedly step the parameters against the gradient. A mini-batch is a random slice of rows per step; an epoch is one pass over all rows; the learning rate is the step size.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Gradient check
cards.a: Comparing the formula's gradient with a brute-force slope from nudging one parameter. Done once per new model.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Standardization
cards.a: Subtract the training mean and divide by the training standard deviation, per column, so features are on one scale.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Regularization
cards.a: Any penalty or constraint that keeps a model from fitting noise: weight decay, leaf limits, feature and row subsampling, early stopping.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Overfitting
cards.a: Fitting the training data's noise so that validation gets worse while training gets better.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Early stopping
cards.a: Stop training when the validation metric has not improved for a while, and keep the best point.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Decision tree
cards.a: A model that asks yes/no questions about features and gives a constant answer in each leaf.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Gradient boosting / LightGBM
cards.a: Hundreds of small trees, each fitted to the errors of the ones before; their sum is the score. LightGBM is the fast library used in production here.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Categorical feature
cards.a: A column of names rather than amounts (station id, direction). Declared so the trees can split on sets of values.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Feature importance / SHAP
cards.a: Importance by gain totals how much each feature reduced the loss; SHAP splits one prediction into per-feature contributions.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Neural network / MLP
cards.a: Layers of weighted sums with a nonlinearity (ReLU) between them. A multilayer perceptron is the plain version.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: ReLU
cards.a: max(z, 0): zeroes negatives. The nonlinearity that lets a network bend.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Backpropagation
cards.a: The chain rule applied layer by layer, backward from the loss, to get every gradient.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: PyTorch / autograd / MPS
cards.a: The deep-learning library; autograd derives gradients automatically; MPS is how it reaches the Mac's GPU.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Optimizer (AdamW)
cards.a: The rule that turns gradients into parameter updates; AdamW adapts the step per parameter and adds weight decay.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Recurrent network / GRU
cards.a: A model that reads a sequence step by step, keeping a hidden state; the GRU uses gates to decide what to remember.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Hidden state
cards.a: The vector a recurrent network carries from step to step: its summary of what it has read.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Adjacency matrix
cards.a: An N × N table of 0/1 saying which stations are neighbors. A @ h sums each station's neighbors' vectors.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Graph neural network / neighbor mixing
cards.a: A model that lets each station read transformed summaries of its neighbors, using the adjacency matrices.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Multi-task
cards.a: One model with several outputs, here the three horizons.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Residual connection
cards.a: Adding a layer's input to its output (h + f(h)), so the layer learns a correction.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Autocorrelation
cards.a: Correlation of a series with itself at a lag; how long the past stays informative.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Fundamental diagram
cards.a: Flow against occupancy: rising while the road is free, falling once it is saturated. Congestion is the falling branch.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Isotonic regression
cards.a: A step function that only goes up, fitted to map raw scores to observed frequencies. The calibration method used.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Atomic write
cards.a: Write to a temporary file, then rename it over the real one, so a reader never sees a half-written file.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Resident memory (RSS)
cards.a: The RAM a process is actually using, logged per stage so a 16 GB machine never swaps.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.
